analysis.one_liner: Caps interest and fees on all consumer credit, including cards and payday loans, at 36%.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap consumer credit rates and fees at 36% was introduced with 3 cosponsors, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to lend to a consumer at a combined cost of interest and fees above 36% a year, covering credit cards, payday loans, car title loans, and bank overdraft fees. Credit cards would have to display one all-in rate, labeled "FAIR," instead of the APR. The bill also lets state attorneys general sue violators and adds criminal penalties of up to a year in prison and large fines.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who borrow at high cost: cardholders paying penalty fees stacked on interest, payday borrowers charged around 400% a year, car title borrowers around 300%, and bank customers hit with overdraft fees the bill's findings estimate cost consumers roughly $14 billion. Anyone paying above 36% all-in would have those charges voided and returned, and state attorneys general could sue on their behalf. The military already has this protection; this bill would extend it to everyone.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a hard 36% ceiling on the combined interest and fees for any consumer loan, including all fees like late fees, overdraft fees, cash advance fees, and add-on insurance, so lenders cannot hide costs outside the rate.

Makes any loan made above 36% unenforceable: the lender must return all principal, interest, and fees, and the borrower can raise the violation as a defense at any time, even during a debt collection or repossession.

Adds enforcement teeth beyond regulators: state attorneys general can sue within three years of a violation, and violators face up to a year in prison and fines of up to three times the debt or $50,000 per violation.
Requires credit card statements to show a single all-in rate labeled 'FAIR' instead of an APR that excludes most fees, so borrowers can see the true yearly cost.
Closes the loopholes that let high-cost lending persist in all 50 states, such as bank-rate exportation and safe harbors for specific loan products, while leaving states free to impose stricter caps.

analysis.who_pays: The lenders that earn revenue above 36%: credit card issuers, especially those relying on late and penalty fees; payday and car title lenders, whose business model the bill's findings put at average rates of 400% and 300%; and banks collecting overdraft fees, which the bill counts toward the 36% cap. Some high-risk borrowers could also lose access to credit if lenders decide those loans are unprofitable at 36%.

drawbacks.text: The 36% ceiling counts penalty fees like late fees, insufficient funds fees, and overdraft fees toward the cap, which would force card issuers to reprice or eliminate fee revenue and could lead them to raise annual fees or tighten approval so that lower-income and subprime customers get fewer card offers.

Lenders who cannot profit at 36% may simply stop serving the highest-risk borrowers, leaving some people with no legal option for emergency cash, which is the standard objection to any usury cap; the bill responds only by stating that affordable alternatives 'should be encouraged,' without funding or mandating any.

The criminal penalties, one year in prison and a fine of up to three times the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation, apply to any person who violates the section or even tries to enforce a covered agreement, which banks warned-style critics would call disproportionate for rate-setting errors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and immediate for the tens of millions of households the bill's own findings show paying roughly $27 billion a year on overdraft, payday, and car title borrowing alone, plus triple-digit-rate online installment loans; charges above 36% would be voided and refunded. The real cost falls on the highest-risk borrowers, who could lose access to credit entirely rather than pay less for it, and on lenders whose fee-driven business models would shrink. A 36% cap has operated for the military since 2006, which the bill cites as evidence it can work, but extending it nationwide without building subsidized alternatives for borrowers banks will not serve at 36% is a genuine gap in the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on September 6, 2023, with Senators Blumenthal, Merkley, and Whitehouse as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.

No further action was ever taken: the committee never scheduled a markup or vote, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and no House action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The lenders that charge above 36%, including credit card issuers collecting penalty fees, payday and car title lenders, and banks collecting overdraft fees, keep their existing revenue because the cap never came to a vote.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee (Chair Sherrod Brown)
against.role: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled it for markup or a vote; it saw no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: High-cost lenders and card issuers
against.role: Credit card, payday, car title, and overdraft-fee industries
against.what_they_did: Industries whose business models depend on rates and fees above 36% have consistently opposed nationwide usury caps of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all four sponsors and all 3 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The cap counts late fees, cash advance fees, over-limit fees, and add-on products toward the 36% limit, wiping out much of the fee revenue card issuers earn from customers who carry balances or miss payments. Issuers would have to reprice or restrict credit to the riskiest borrowers.

The bill's findings put these loans at roughly 400% and 300% average annual rates, so a 36% cap with no product exemptions would effectively end the storefront and online versions of this lending. Borrowers who rely on these loans would need some other source of small-dollar credit.

Overdraft and insufficient funds fees count toward the 36% cap, which the bill's findings estimate costs consumers about $14 billion a year at effective rates it puts near 17,000%. Banks would lose this fee income or have to shrink overdraft programs.
